description: We are school students from Pune, India, passionate about science, space exploration and technology. We are curious, creative and eager to solve real-world problems using NASA's open data. We enjoy teamwork, research and learning new skills. We are looking for teammates interested in science, astronomy, coding, data analysis, design and creative problem-solving. Beginners are welcome!
summary:
SPACE RELICS is my digital museum exploring NASA equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars. I have selected four historic machines: the Apollo Lunar Module, Lunar Roving Vehicle, Sojourner Rover and Ingenuity Helicopter.

Through illustrated stories, mission timelines and scientific facts, I explore why these machines were sent, what they achieved, why they were left behind and what they taught humanity about space exploration.

Using NASA's Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA) and NASA mission resources, I connect historical missions with the future of space science.

My aim is to make space exploration interesting and understandable for students and inspire the next generation of scientists and explorers.
details:
SPACE RELICS

The Forgotten Machines of the Moon and Mars

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

Created and researched by: Zainab Khokhawala
Location: Pune, India

1. Introduction

When humans explore space, they send machines millions of kilometres away to help them discover new worlds. Some machines return to Earth, but many remain where their missions took place.

The Moon and Mars contain equipment left behind by some of humanity's greatest space missions. These machines may no longer be operational, but their stories, discoveries and scientific contributions remain important.

I created SPACE RELICS to explore the stories behind these forgotten machines and understand why they were sent into space, what they achieved and why they remain on other worlds.

My project focuses on four remarkable examples: the Apollo Lunar Module, the Lunar Roving Vehicle, the Sojourner Mars Rover and the Ingenuity Mars Helicopter.

2. My Research Objectives

Through this project, I wanted to:

  1. Discover what NASA equipment remains on the Moon and Mars.
  2. Understand the purpose and scientific importance of each machine.
  3. Explore how these machines contributed to space exploration.
  4. Understand why their missions ended and what happened to the equipment afterwards.
  5. Present scientific information in a simple and interesting way for other students.
3. The Moon: Machines That Remained Behind

A. Apollo Lunar Module

Mission: Apollo 15
Lunar Module name: Falcon
Location: Hadley-Apennine region, Moon
Year: 1971

The Apollo Lunar Module was designed to transport astronauts from lunar orbit to the Moon's surface.

During Apollo 15, astronauts David Scott and James Irwin used the Lunar Module Falcon to descend to the lunar surface. After completing their exploration, the ascent stage lifted off to rejoin the Command and Service Module in lunar orbit.

The descent stage remained on the Moon.

Why it matters:

The Lunar Module demonstrated that humans could travel from lunar orbit to the surface of another world and return. Its design and engineering became an important milestone in human space exploration.

What I discovered:

I found it fascinating that a spacecraft could be divided into two parts, with one part returning to orbit while the other remained permanently on the Moon.

B. Lunar Roving Vehicle

Missions: Apollo 15, Apollo 16 and Apollo 17
Location: Moon
Years: 1971–1972

The Lunar Roving Vehicle, commonly called the Moon buggy, was a battery-powered electric vehicle designed to transport astronauts across the lunar surface.

Before the rover, astronauts had to explore relatively small areas around their landing sites. The rover allowed them to travel farther, carry scientific equipment and collect more geological samples.

Three Lunar Roving Vehicles were used during the final three Apollo lunar landing missions. They were left on the Moon after the missions ended.

Why it matters:

The rover increased the distance astronauts could explore and helped scientists collect more information about lunar geology.

What I discovered:

I learned that even a relatively small vehicle can make a huge difference to scientific exploration when it is designed for an entirely different environment.

4. Mars: Robots That Explored Another Planet

C. Sojourner Mars Rover

Mission: Mars Pathfinder
Landing date: 4 July 1997
Location: Mars

Sojourner was the first successful robotic rover to operate on Mars.

It was a small, six-wheeled vehicle that explored the Martian surface, photographed rocks and soil, and conducted scientific investigations.

One of its important instruments was the Alpha Proton X-ray Spectrometer, which helped scientists study the chemical composition of rocks and soil.

The rover was originally planned for a seven-day mission but operated for 83 days.

Communication with the Pathfinder lander eventually ended, and the mission was formally terminated in March 1998.

Why it matters:

Sojourner demonstrated that a small robotic vehicle could successfully explore another planet. It helped establish the importance of mobile robotic exploration for future Mars missions.

What I discovered:

I was surprised that a rover designed for only seven days continued working for 83 days. Its mission showed how much scientific value can come from even a small robotic explorer.

D. Ingenuity Mars Helicopter

Mission: Mars 2020
Location: Jezero Crater, Mars
First flight: 19 April 2021
Final flight: 18 January 2024

Ingenuity was one of NASA's most extraordinary experiments.

It became the first aircraft to achieve powered, controlled flight on another planet.

Originally designed to complete up to five experimental flights, Ingenuity eventually completed 72 flights over almost three years.

It demonstrated that powered flight was possible in the thin Martian atmosphere and helped scientists and engineers understand how aerial vehicles could support planetary exploration.

During its 72nd flight, the helicopter sustained rotor damage during landing and was no longer capable of flying.

It remains on Mars.

Why it matters:

Ingenuity opened up new possibilities for aerial exploration. Its technology demonstration could help future missions explore difficult terrain from the air.

What I discovered:

I found it incredible that an aircraft designed for just five test flights completed 72 flights on another planet.

These machines had different purposes, but each helped humanity understand how to explore worlds beyond Earth.

6. Why Were These Machines Left Behind?

Space missions have strict limitations involving fuel, weight, power, technology and mission design.

Returning every piece of equipment to Earth is not always necessary or practical.

Some equipment is designed to remain on the surface after its useful mission is complete. Other machines become inactive because of technical failures, communication loss or environmental damage.

I learned that being left behind does not necessarily mean that a mission failed.

A mission can end while its scientific contribution continues to benefit future generations.

7. The Scientific Legacy

The four machines featured in SPACE RELICS represent important achievements in engineering and science.

Their contributions include:

  • Developing technology for landing and travelling on other worlds.
  • Improving our understanding of lunar and Martian surfaces.
  • Demonstrating the value of robotic exploration.
  • Testing new technologies for future planetary missions.
  • Inspiring future scientists, engineers and space explorers.

Their physical missions may have ended, but the knowledge gained from them continues to influence space exploration.

8. My Research Methodology

I organised my research around four NASA missions and their associated equipment.

My research process involved:

  1. Identifying the machines listed in the NASA Space Apps Challenge resources.
  2. Studying their mission histories and scientific purposes.
  3. Exploring NASA's Space Science Data Coordinated Archive.
  4. Reviewing NASA mission descriptions and historical records.
  5. Comparing the machines based on their purpose, achievements and final status.
  6. Organising the findings into a student-friendly digital presentation.

I selected these four machines because they represent different stages of human exploration, from landing astronauts on the Moon to flying an aircraft on Mars.

9. My Conclusion

Before working on this project, I thought of abandoned space equipment simply as machines that had stopped working or completed their missions.

I now understand that these machines are also part of the history of scientific discovery.

Each one represents years of planning, engineering, experimentation and courage.

The Lunar Module helped humans reach the Moon. The Lunar Roving Vehicle helped astronauts explore farther. Sojourner demonstrated the possibilities of robotic exploration, while Ingenuity proved that powered flight could take place on another planet.

Through SPACE RELICS, I wanted to show that space exploration is not only about reaching new places. It is also about the knowledge, discoveries and technology we leave behind.

A machine may be forgotten on another world, but its contribution to science should never be forgotten.

I used publicly available NASA educational and mission resources as the basis for my research.

ChatGPT was used as an AI-assisted tool to help organise the project structure, improve language and prepare presentation drafts. I reviewed the material and am responsible for the final research, selection of information and presentation.
